title: Senate approves permitting bill with nuclear energy amendments—what’s next?
summary: Just before Congress left Washington, D.C., for the Thanksgiving holiday, the U.S. Senate passed a permitting reform bill that would overhaul the permitting process for numerous types of energy projects—including those in and around nuclear energy—to get projects off the ground and completed in less time. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) passed the Senate on November 19 with a 62–33 vote. The legislation now heads to the U.S. House and to a lame-duck chamber, where its fate remains uncertain. Whether it successfully passes or is not enacted into law, BAAJA will have an impact on future nuclear energy projects, as the bill addresses specific nuclear topics in a series of amendments made ahead of the Senate vote.

title: INL chooses Guidedwave for fuel canister monitoring demo at SONGS
summary: The Center for Used Fuel Research at Idaho National Laboratory has announced that it will use acoustic emissions (AE) technology from development firm Guidedwave in an upcoming demonstration project. The project will test the ability of Guidedwave’s AE sensors to provide continuous, automated monitoring of a simulation nuclear fuel canister at San Onofre Nuclear Generating Station (SONGS) in California, a facility that permanently ceased operating in 2013. The dry storage canister will be fitted with electric heaters and will not contain nuclear waste. The demo will last for one year, beginning in February 2027.

title: Sandia researchers are developing SPINE robot for Hanford Site cleanup
summary: The ongoing nuclear waste cleanup efforts at Washington state’s Hanford Site may soon get a boost from robots developed at Sandia National Laboratories. Led by mechanical engineer Steve Buerger, a team at Sandia has created a two-inch-by-six-inch robotic device called SPINE (Self-Propelled Interior Inspector for Nondestructive-Testing Examination) to crawl through and inspect aging pipes that link one underground storage tank to another at Hanford.

title: Pacific Fusion Gets Key Licence For $1 Billion New Mexico Demonstration Facility
summary: US-based Pacific Fusion announced that the New Mexico Environment Department (NMED) has approved its radioactive materials licence, enabling the company to operate a fusion machine and accelerate its efforts to bring fusion energy to the grid. The licence authorises Pacific Fusion to possess and use tritium for fusion at its $1bn (€910m) research and manufacturing campus in Albuquerque, a facility that will house its demonstration fusion system. The company said this is the first radioactive materials licence New Mexico has ever issued to a private fusion company, and enables key research supporting the company’s goal of net facility gain by 2030, generating more energy output than the energy used to power the system.
